The Mekong River. Southeast Asia's longest and most important river, flowing approximately forty-three hundred fifty kilometers from its source in the Tibetan Plateau through six countries before emptying into the South China Sea via a vast delta in Vietnam. It is the economic and cultural artery of mainland Southeast Asia, supporting over sixty million people through fishing, agriculture, and trade.

The Mekong originates in the Tibetan Plateau and flows southeast through China, Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia, Thailand, and Vietnam. The Mekong Delta in southern Vietnam is one of the world's most productive agricultural regions, supplying rice, fish, and coconut to global markets. Tonle Sap Lake in Cambodia is connected to the Mekong and experiences one of the world's largest seasonal water-level fluctuations. The river is home to the Irrawaddy dolphin, a freshwater cetacean, and the Mekong giant catfish, both critically endangered species endemic to the river.

The Khone Falls in Laos are the largest waterfall system in Southeast Asia, creating a natural barrier to navigation. Controversial dams, particularly in China and Laos, disrupt fish migration and alter seasonal flooding patterns that farmers depend on. The Mekong River Commission, established in nineteen ninety-five, manages shared resources among riparian nations.
